parts.label: Understand
parts.title: Buy evidence in stages
parts.body:
AI investment has several kinds of uncertainty: whether the workflow matters, whether a system can perform it, whether people will use it safely, and whether value survives at scale. A stage gate matches spending to the uncertainty the next stage can retire. Discovery documents the workflow, baseline, affected people, and plausible options. A prototype tests feasibility on representative cases. Controlled production tests real adoption, cost, quality, and controls. Scale adds operational support, local variations, and continued monitoring.

Write each gate before entering the stage. Specify the evidence, decision maker, spending ceiling, and options to continue, narrow, redesign, or stop. The requirements should grow with the possible impact and reversibility of the use. A low-risk internal drafting aid and a system that affects access to a public service need different evidence and approval routes. NIST's Map, Measure, and Manage functions give a useful structure for tying context and evaluation to a risk response.

Stopping can be an informed result. If a prototype exposes a fundamental data gap, continuing to spend on interface polish will not repair the investment case. Record why the team stopped so another team does not repeat the same experiment.

example.title: A discovery gate
example.body: A service team seeks funding to automate claim triage. Discovery has identified 12,000 monthly eligible cases, a 22-minute baseline, an owner, and a sample of difficult cases. The next $40,000, an illustrative cap, buys a prototype that must meet agreed quality on that sample. It does not authorize live decisions about claims.

exercise.title: Create a gate table
exercise.body: For one use case, write four rows: discovery, prototype, controlled production, scale. Give each the maximum spend, evidence required, decision maker, and one explicit stop or redesign condition.

sources: NIST AI RMF Core: Map, Measure, Manage
OECD AI Principles: risk management over the lifecycle

parts.label: Practice
parts.title: Set a gate for a claims summarizer
parts.body:
Imagine a summarizer that drafts a source-linked claim file for a human examiner. On a small test set it saves preparation time, yet it sometimes attributes a conclusion to the wrong document. The next gate must examine the failure, not average it away. Define representative cases, including long files, conflicting documents, missing records, and the languages the organization serves. Grade whether every material assertion has a correct supporting citation and whether the examiner catches errors.

A controlled pilot can keep human review mandatory, restrict its case types, cap volume, and preserve the old process as fallback. Set a citation error threshold before testing; the appropriate number depends on the harm of an error and the reliability of review. The pilot should measure net examiner time, correction burden, and consequential mistakes as well as model output quality. If citations fail the threshold, fund redesign or stop. If quality passes but adoption is poor, investigate workflow fit before expansion.

The owner of the claims decision remains accountable even when a vendor provides the model. The CAIO can set the common evidence method; a product leader and relevant risk owners decide whether this specific use is ready within their authorities.

example.title: A gate memo with a real choice
example.body: Illustrative decision: fund a six-week, 200-case supervised pilot under a $25,000 cap. Every summary receives examiner review. Pause if a material unsupported assertion reaches a final decision or if citation error exceeds the preset threshold in the audit sample. The pilot's result determines whether to redesign retrieval, extend testing, or seek wider authorization.

exercise.title: Define three outcomes
exercise.body: Write the evidence that would justify scale, redesign, or cancellation for the claims summarizer. Name the evaluation set, quality criterion, human review burden, business outcome, owner, and date of the next decision.

sources: NIST AI RMF Core: risk response and monitored operation

parts.label: Operate
parts.title: Run gates without freezing the portfolio
parts.body:
A gate meeting should decide what to fund next, rather than replay the entire project history. Ask the sponsor to provide a one-page record: original hypothesis, spend to date, baseline, observed results, open risks, revised forecast, and a recommendation. Reviewers can inspect the underlying evidence and return a decision with conditions. Time-box the review according to the organization's risk and funding process.

Keep three authorities distinct. The business sponsor owns value and adoption. Technical and risk functions review the evidence and can exercise their established control authority. The investment body releases funds within its remit. A CAIO coordinates the portfolio and common evaluation method, but a title alone does not transfer legal, financial, or security powers. Escalation rules should say what happens when a sponsor wants to proceed despite a failed metric.

Continue monitoring after scale. NIST includes post-deployment monitoring, override, incident response, change management, and decommissioning within risk management. A material change in use, population, data, model, or autonomy should send the project back through the appropriate review. Otherwise a successful narrow pilot can quietly become a different system.

example.title: A changed scope
example.body: A summarizer approved for internal drafting is proposed for customer-visible explanations. The output audience and potential harm have changed. The sponsor brings customer comprehension, error, privacy, and response evidence to a new gate instead of treating the earlier approval as reusable.

exercise.title: Design a decision log
exercise.body: Create fields for stage, scope, evidence version, decision, conditions, risk acceptor, spending authorization, expiry or review date, and change triggers. Draft a sample entry for an approval with one condition.

sources: NIST AI RMF Core: Govern and Manage 4.1

parts.label: Apply
parts.title: Allocate a constrained portfolio
parts.body:
A CAIO rarely gets enough funding for every promising proposal. Compare candidates by expected value, evidence quality, risk, strategic fit, dependency, and the cost of the next informative experiment. Do not force them into a single precise score that hides different kinds of uncertainty. Show the board or investment committee a small set of choices and what each dollar will establish. A cheap experiment that resolves a decisive assumption may deserve priority over a large rollout with a glossy forecast.

Sequence shared investments with use cases. Funding retrieval infrastructure before anyone has validated a workflow can strand capacity. Funding a dozen isolated pilots without shared controls can create expensive duplication. A paired proposal can fund one bounded use case and the reusable capability it actually needs, with separate owners and success criteria.

The portfolio should include an exit reserve for pilots that fail and operating funds for those that scale. Forecasts that count all projected benefit but omit monitoring, support, and retirement will look attractive only until the first production incident. Record how much of the budget is committed, contingent at a gate, or available for new evidence.

example.title: Three candidates
example.body: An illustrative committee has $500,000. A low-risk internal drafting pilot asks $60,000 to test workflow benefit; a customer assistant asks $180,000 for controlled production after quality testing; a decision aid asks $400,000 but lacks representative data. The committee can fund the first two with separate gates and reserve the rest while the third sponsor resolves its data gap.

exercise.title: Write the allocation note
exercise.body: Select two of three hypothetical proposals under a fixed budget. State the next uncertainty each tranche buys, the evidence threshold, spend cap, accountable sponsor, dependency, and what happens to the uncommitted funds. Defend the choice without inventing a precise ROI for untested systems.

sources: NIST AI RMF Core: documented risk responses
